newsitem.title: FRANCE: Dasa, Snecma, Fiat join in jet engine bid.
newsitem.headline: Dasa, Snecma, Fiat join in jet engine bid.

text.p: The aircraft engine unit of Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG said on Monday it was partnering French and Italian firms in a bid to produce military aricraft engines.

Dasa's Motoren- und Turbinen-Union (MTU), French engine maker Snecma and Italy's FiatAvio would work together to bid to supply engines for a future European transport plane, MTU said at a news conference at the Paris airshow.

Reflecting a drive to consolidate Europe's aircraft industry, the partners are considering turning the partnership into an independent corporation and hope it could form the basis for a single military jet engine company incorporating all major European suppliers, MTU chief Rainer Hertrich said.

"In the future I think there will be only one military house in Europe with all major partners taking a share," he said. "I think that would be an important project to close the gap between Europe and the Americans."

Also at the airshow, MTU said it agreed to work with state-owned Snecma to study technology to reduce fuel consumption in civil jet engines and signed a contract worth 500 million marks over two years to maintain engines for courier Federal Express.
In addition, MTU said it was expanding cooperation with Volvo Aero, with each partner now concentrating on developing and producing specific engine parts.
MTU, Snecma and FiatAvio signed a memorandum of understanding to produce the M138 engine required for the future transport aircraft (FTA), a project involving eight countries.
The three companies were also talking to other prospective partners and were making "good headway", Hertrich said.
"We are willing to turn the team into a single corporate identity," he said. "This could be the core of one military engine house in the future."

Other officials from Dasa, part of German industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG, and British Aerospace Plc made similar appeals over the weekend for Europe's aerospace groups to move together in one multinational group.

American contractors have gained competitive strength recently through a series of mergers, pressuring Europe's fractured aerospace industry to consolidate to reduce costs and excess production capacity.
While MTU sought a European solution in military engines, it wanted to continue cooperating with North American partners in civil aviation, Hertrich said.
In the study with Snecma, MTU hoped to find out if new technology could cut fuel consuption by 20 percent in engines for long-haul civil aircraft.
Hertrich said the technology involved reheating exhaust but declined to give further details.
In its cooperation with Volvo Aero, MTU agreed to focus on jet blades, disk and rings, while Volvo designed and produced casings.
